![](../../img/conversation_2780E3.svg){.page-art}

*An in-class activity. Nothing to turn in and no answer key -- this one needs
other people, which is why it happens in class rather than at home.*

**The idea.** A population is defined by the question you are asking, not by the
data you happened to collect -- and the gap is far easier to see in someone
else's study than in your own.

**Format.** About 10 minutes · pairs · no laptop needed.

## 1. Write one (3 minutes)

On a half sheet of paper, describe a study **from your own area** in two or three
sentences. Say what you want to know and exactly how you would recruit. Use no
statistical vocabulary, and do not name the population -- just the recruitment.

Put your name on it and hand it to your partner.

## 2. Take theirs apart (5 minutes)

Working from your partner's paper alone:

- Name the **target population** their question implies.
- Name the **sampled population** their recruitment would actually produce.
- Name one specific way a parameter could differ between the two.
- Decide whether a larger $n$ would close the gap you found, or leave it exactly
  where it is.

Hand it back. The author's job is to say whether the gap is fair -- and if it is,
whether they would have caught it themselves.

## 3. Whole class (2 minutes)

- Whose partner found a gap the author had not thought of? Two examples.
- Show of hands: how many of the gaps found in this room would a larger sample
  fix?

*If you have more time: two labs sample the same population and report means of
1.3 and 1.9. List everything that could cause that, then sort the list into
"would shrink with more data" and "would not."*

{{< dstart summary="If you were not in class" >}}

The hands almost never go up, and that is the point: **a larger $n$ shrinks
sampling error and does nothing at all to a mismatch between the population you
sampled and the one you meant to describe.** A study of 10,000 undergraduates is
still a study of undergraduates.

The reason this runs on someone else's study rather than a textbook vignette is
that the gap in a vignette is planted and findable, while the gap in your own
design is invisible to you -- you already know who you meant, so the recruitment
sentence reads as though it says so. Your partner has only the words on the page,
which is also all a reviewer will have.
